articles.title: Trump promised 300,000 tons of beef imports at lower tariff rates to reduce grocery costs. Instead, shipments have lagged and prices haven’t budged
articles.summary: “The simple assumption there was that if we can just increase supply of beef in the U.S., that should lower prices. Unfortunately, the beef industry is much...
articles.body:
At the nexus of an ongoing affordability crisis and midterm election push, the Trump administration's effort to reduce beef prices appears to be falling short.

President Donald Trump signed a proclamation in August to temporarily increase the quantity of beef in the U.S. by importing 300,000 metric tons of lean beef trimmings into the country at a reduced tariff rate. The imports were scheduled over 90 days, from September through November.

"This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again," Trump wrote on Truth Social announcing the policy.

But as of Oct. 19, the U.S. has imported just 59,423 metric tons of beef, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data , or just 20% of the target. And ground beef averaged $6.79 per pound as of September, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data , down from $6.92 in August, but still above $6.32 a year ago.

This 7% year-over-year increase in beef, due to persistently high demand as well as dwindling herd sizes, has far outpaced the 2.5%-2.9% hike in overall U.S. grocery prices, which has become representative of America's affordability woes. Trump has identified beef prices as a key issue to address during the second half of his term, as he targets policy toward the typically loyal Republican base of farmers.

"It really became unacceptable to the voter," Trump said last month. "And we do have to get elected, because if we're not going to get elected, your ranchers and your farmers are in big trouble."

But both farmers and agricultural economists are doubtful that 300,000 tons of imported beef will deliver price cuts, arguing the initiative is ineffective at best, and a financial strain during an already challenging period for the industry at worst.

"The simple assumption there was that if we can just increase supply of beef in the U.S., that should lower prices," Derrell Peel, a professor of agribusiness specializing in livestock at Oklahoma State University, told Fortune . "Unfortunately, the beef industry is much more complex than that."

The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune 's request for comment.

Why Trump's push for lower beef costs are falling short

Part of why Americans aren't seeing a noticeable difference in beef costs is because the type of beef being sent from overseas doesn't typically hit retail shelves, Peel noted. Lean beef trimmings are often combined with fatty trimmings produced from cattle in American feed lots. This combination of beef is usually used by fast food restaurants, not grocery stores where many American consumers are looking for relief.

images.caption: President Donald Trump announced a policy in September to increase beef imports with the goal of lowering prices. · Fortune · Kent NISHIMURA/AFP—Getty Images

articles.title: US-Canada Trade Talks Are Picking Up Pace But No Deal Yet, Carney Says
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said trade talks with the US have gained a bit of momentum, and suggested that any progress has been because the Trump ad...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said trade talks with the US have gained a bit of momentum, and suggested that any progress has been because the Trump administration has shown more flexibility.

Speaking to reporters in Ottawa on Monday, Carney said "there's a slight intensification" in trade discussions. That followed comments from President Donald Trump and one of his advisers over the weekend that the two nations were getting closer to some kind of agreement.

US and Canadian officials negotiated for weeks over the summer, but the talks broke down on Aug. 21, leading Trump to put 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of goods from Canada. Canada retaliated with counter-tariffs on a similar value of US products.

The Canadian prime minister said Monday he would still refuse to agree to what the US was offering in August, which would have kept US tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos but at lower rates. That round of talks collapsed in part over a disagreement about whether the US would extend tariff relief to medium- and heavy-duty trucks.

"We have very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August," Carney said. "To the extent any progress has been made, it's because the US is coming closer to our position."

White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett told Fox News on Sunday that trade negotiations with Canada were gaining steam. "I think it's very close to finally having a deal on that," he said, two days after the US modified some of its tariffs on imports from Canada to benefit Maine businesses following lobbying by Senator Susan Collins.

Talks have picked up between Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's minister responsible for the negotiations with the US, in recent weeks and are ongoing, another US official said Sunday, adding that prospects remain unclear since the US doesn't believe Canada is offering enough yet.

Trump also told Detroit's Fox 2 channel on Sunday that "we're getting close to a deal, and a deal could happen that's going to be very good for everybody."

articles.title: CRP apura conduta de psicóloga que falou sobre não contratar petistas | G1
articles.standfirst: Conselho afirmou que processos seletivos devem usar apenas critérios técnicos. CRP informou que vai encaminhar o caso para apuração do Código de Processamento Disciplinar.
articles.summary: Conselho afirmou que processos seletivos devem usar apenas critérios técnicos. CRP informou que vai encaminhar o caso para apuração do Código de Processamento Disciplinar.
articles.body:
O Conselho Regional de Psicologia (CRP) de Goiás emitiu uma nota repudiando a discriminação político-partidária na seleção de trabalhadores, nesta terça-feira (27). O posicionamento foi emitido após a psicóloga Mara Suassuna publicar um vídeo em suas redes sociais falando sobre não selecionar candidatos "petistas" para vagas de emprego.

Ao g1 , Suassuna afirmou que fundamentou sua declaração na teoria desenvolvida pelo psicólogo Shalom H. Schwartz, que aborda valores básicos do ser humano e como isso orienta escolhas de comportamento (confira as notas completas ao final do texto).

💡 A Legislação Trabalhista proíbe qualquer tipo de discriminação e que limite o acesso à relação de trabalho, podendo gerar multas e sanções econômicas.

O CRP também incluiu na manifestação partes do Código de Ética da profissão em que afirma que a psicologia deve contribuir para a eliminação de discriminações, e proíbe praticar ou ser conivente com atos discriminatórios, "bem como induzir a convicções políticas ou ideológicas no exercício profissional".

No vídeo, Suassuna afirma ter uma empresa de recrutamentos e que tem sido procurada por empresários , logo após o resultado das eleições, interessados em contratar colaboradores que seguissem o critério político.

"Os nossos valores são fundamentais para que as escolhas sejam feitas. E por isso, empresários, CEOs de empresas, as pessoas que estão por aí gerando as riquezas do Brasil têm que se preocupar sim em contratar pessoas que tenham os mesmos valores", afirmou.

Sobre isso, o CRP afirmou que os processos de recrutamento e seleção de profissionais realizados por psicólogos devem se basear exclusivamente em critérios técnicos relacionados a exigências do cargo, sem que seja legitimada a exclusão de pessoas.

O conselho concluiu a nota informando que vai encaminhar o caso para apuração do Código de Processamento Disciplinar.

Ao g1 , profissionais da área discordaram do posicionamento de Mara. Luísa Jaques Côrtes, especializada em psicanálise e análise do contemporâneo, destacou que a fala de Suassuna é "problemática".

"Posso afirmar que acho muito problemática uma afirmação como essa, ainda mais instrumentalizada pela psicologia, se esse for o caso [...]. Me chama muita atenção, como sempre, após eleições a utilização de falas como essas voltam a circular", disse a profissional.

A psicóloga Iara Caixeta Moreira, que atua na área social comunitária em atenção a vítimas de violações de direito, também criticou o posicionamento de Mara Suassuna e defendeu a diversidade de pensamento.

"Defender a diversidade de pensamento exige mais do que afirmar que pensar diferente é legítimo. Exige reconhecer que pessoas com diferentes trajetórias, convicções e visões de mundo podem compartilhar compromissos profissionais fundamentais".

"Não se trata de pensar igual. Trata-se de compartilhar princípios.

A Teoria dos Valores Humanos Básicos, desenvolvida pelo psicólogo Shalom H. Schwartz, demonstra que nossos valores orientam escolhas, comportamentos, prioridades e decisões.

Nas amizades, nas relações profissionais e nas organizações, a compatibilidade de valores favorece a confiança, o pertencimento e a construção de objetivos comuns.

Após os resultados das eleições, muitos empresários têm procurado o Instituto Mara Suassuna para novos processos seletivos, destacando o alinhamento de valores como critério decisivo na contratação.

Mas atenção: alinhamento de valores organizacionais não significa alinhamento político. Significa identificar profissionais que compartilhem princípios como ética, responsabilidade, respeito, integridade e compromisso com os objetivos da empresa.

A diversidade de pensamento fortalece as organizações. O que compromete os resultados não é pensar diferente, mas agir em desacordo com os princípios que sustentam a cultura organizacional.

Sugiro conhecer a teoria de Schwartz. Afinal, nossos valores orientam nossas escolhas, e nossas escolhas revelam quem somos."

"O Conselho Regional de Psicologia da 9ª Região (CRP-09) tomou conhecimento de vídeo, amplamente divulgado nas redes sociais e na imprensa, em que se defende a adoção de critérios político-partidários na seleção de trabalhadoras e trabalhadores.

O CRP-09 repudia, de forma veemente, qualquer forma de discriminação no acesso ao trabalho, inclusive por convicção política. Essa prática é vedada pela Constituição Federal (arts. 3º, IV, 5º, VIII, e 7º, XXX), pela Convenção nº 111 da Organização Internacional do Trabalho, ratificada pelo Brasil, e pela Lei nº 9.029/1995.

O Código de Ética Profissional do Psicólogo é igualmente claro. A Psicologia deve contribuir para a eliminação de quaisquer formas de discriminação, e é vedado à psicóloga e ao psicólogo praticar ou ser conivente com atos discriminatórios, bem como induzir a convicções políticas ou ideológicas no exercício profissional.

Processos de recrutamento e seleção conduzidos por profissionais da Psicologia devem se basear exclusivamente em critérios técnicos relacionados às exigências do cargo, nunca na orientação política, partidária ou ideológica de candidatas e candidatos. O conhecimento psicológico não pode ser instrumentalizado para legitimar a exclusão de pessoas.

Diante dos fatos, o CRP-09 adotará de imediato as providências de sua competência, com o encaminhamento do caso para apuração nos termos do Código de Processamento Disciplinar.

Os procedimentos disciplinares tramitam em sigilo, nos termos do art. 15 da Resolução CFP nº 11/2019, assegurados o contraditório e a ampla defesa. Por essa razão, o CRP-09 não divulgará outras informações sobre o caso."

articles.title: Multas para autopropelidos em Taubaté: Câmara mantém veto | G1
articles.standfirst: Decisão foi unânime e mantém trecho da lei municipal que previa punições fora das regras do Código de Trânsito Brasileiro.
articles.summary: Multas para autopropelidos em Taubaté seguem as regras do CTB após a Câmara manter veto a punições municipais que entravam em conflito com a legislação federal.
articles.body:
Os vereadores de Taubaté mantiveram, por unanimidade, o veto parcial do prefeito Sérgio Victor (Novo) a um trecho da lei municipal que estabelece regras para a circulação de veículos autopropelidos na cidade. A parte vetada previa punições para quem descumprisse as normas.

Apesar da decisão, algumas infrações de trânsito continuam sujeitas a multas, conforme as regras do Código de Trânsito Brasileiro (CTB).

Segundo a Prefeitura, a Procuradoria municipal apontou uma inconsistência no trecho da lei que criava as penalidades. Isso porque as regras de trânsito são estabelecidas pelo CTB, e o município não pode criar multas que entrem em conflito com a legislação federal.

Com a manutenção do veto, o trecho que previa multas específicas na legislação municipal deixa de valer. No entanto, as infrações que já estão previstas no Código de Trânsito Brasileiro continuam sujeitas às penalidades estabelecidas pela legislação nacional.

Um exemplo é a condução de veículos autopropelidos sem capacete, quando o equipamento é exigido pelas regras aplicáveis ao veículo.

A legislação municipal de Taubaté também prevê medidas como a retenção do veículo em determinadas situações, como nos casos de circulação por menores de 16 anos, conforme as regras previstas na lei.

O veto foi mantido por unanimidade. A lei municipal já está em vigor em Taubaté.

articles.title: Trump announces $250M-plus initiative to recruit, retain nursing home nurses
articles.summary: President Trump announced Monday an initiative worth hundreds of millions of dollars to recruit and retain nursing home nurses. “The Trump Administration is proud to announce a 250 MILLION DOLLAR PLUS initiative to RECRUIT and RETAIN Nurses for Nursing Homes!” Trump said in a Truth Social post Monday evening. “This Federal and State Initiative will…
articles.body:
President Trump announced Monday an initiative worth hundreds of millions of dollars to recruit and retain nursing home nurses.

“The Trump Administration is proud to announce a 250 MILLION DOLLAR PLUS initiative to RECRUIT and RETAIN Nurses for Nursing Homes!” Trump said in a Truth Social post Monday evening.

“This Federal and State Initiative will support thousands and thousands of Nurses and Nursing Students Nationwide, including those serving rural communities,” the president added.

Trump said in the post that the initiative will be under the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) and that it will provide nurses “up to $50,000 in Grants for working in rural communities or understaffed facilities.”

“This Fund was nearly a THIRD of this amount until I stepped in, and had our Great Governors join the fight. Now many more of our Incredible Nurses can be rewarded for helping our Fantastic Seniors,” the president said.

Earlier this month , Senate Democrats published aims of overhauling the American long-term care system, including both home care and nursing homes.

“It has been decades since Congress enacted a comprehensive, system-level investment in long-term care infrastructure and financing. And a system-level investment is what is needed.” Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) said at the time.

articles.title: Apple releases macOS 27.2 Golden Gate: Features, how to download and more
articles.summary: Apple has released latest macOS 27.2 Golden Gate software, marking the first major update to macOS 27 since its launch in September this year.
articles.body: Apple has released latest macOS 27.2 Golden Gate software, marking the first major update to macOS 27 since its launch in September this year. Among other changes, the update brings changes to brightness and volume sliders. It also expands Siri AI to new languages including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. In its release notes, Apple said: “This update provides enhancements to Siri AI with the ability to retain useful context from previous Siri interactions as well as draw from a wider range of personal context. It also introduces Suggestions in Messages that help you take quick actions in apps like Calendar and Reminders based on context from your conversation. This release includes additional features, bug fixes, and security updates for your Mac”.How to download macOS 27.2 Golden GateTo download the macOS 27.2 Golden Gate on your MacBook, follow the steps below:Click the Apple menu in the top-left corner of your screen.Open System Settings.Click General and select Software Update.Wait for your MacBook to check for available updates.If macOS 27.2 Golden Gate is available for your device, click Upgrade Now or Update Now.Enter your administrator password if prompted and follow the on-screen instructions to complete the installation.macOS 27 Golden Gate featuresFirst announced at WWDC in June this year, the macOS 27 Golden Gate software update features a transparency slider that runs from completely clear to fully tinted, so you pick your poison. Sidebars stretch to the edge of the window with refraction continuing underneath them, sidebar icons keep their colour, and every window shares the same corner radius—even apps that haven't been updated. App icons pick up extra Liquid Glass layers built directly into the artwork.A rebuilt search index for Spotlight, Photos and MailThe plumbing behind Spotlight, Photos and Mail has been rearchitected. Right-click on any window or item to ask Siri about it directly, or select multiple files in Finder and have it compare them for you. articles.title: US Plans Two-Month Extension to Shipping-Fee Truce With China
articles.summary: The US may extend a pause on charges for Chinese-linked ships for calling at American ports by two months, following efforts to iron out broader trade issues...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The US may extend a pause on charges for Chinese-linked ships for calling at American ports by two months, following efforts to iron out broader trade issues between the two economies.

If approved, the Office of the United States Trade Representative's proposal will prolong a bilateral truce that was set to expire in early November until Jan. 9, according to a USTR notice issued on Monday. That agreement suspended tit-for-tat port charges that Washington and Beijing had imposed on each other earlier in 2025.

"The United States is continuing to engage with China with the goal of obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices at issue in the investigation," Jennifer Thornton, general counsel for the USTR, said in the notice.

The two-month extension follows a broader trade truce between Washington and Beijing that was announced last month as Chinese President Xi Jinping landed in the US for his first visit in 11 years.

The reciprocal fees imposed last year meant that Chinese- or US-linked ships faced millions of dollars of charges for calling at each others' ports. The penalties forced shipping companies to rejig global operations, and pushed up freight costs. A major South Korean shipbuilder also came under fire, with Beijing sanctioning the company's US units in retaliation for Washington's moves.

articles.title: Data center backlash is uniting America
articles.summary: Candidates’ positions on data center guardrails and moratoriums could play key roles in close elections in Texas, Pennsylvania, and others.
articles.body: If there’s one issue that seems to activate all kinds of voters in 2026, it’s data centers. The rapid buildout of these massive server storage facilities — and the infrastructure construction and expenses that come with them — has sparked local opposition in communities across the country and become a major issue in many congressional and gubernatorial campaigns. At the same time, tech money has been pouring into many of these races. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, has already spent $45 million in a year. And Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed group that says it supports AI safeguards, says it’s raised $80 million. Both have funded Democratic and Republican-aligned groups. Other super PACs see an opportunity to push for stricter AI policies, like the recently created Tomorrow Together, which launched $4 million in ads for battleground House races, with messages about data center development and AI safety. All sorts of candidates appear to be distancing themselves from data centers and taking steps to assuage voters’ concerns about unconstrained buildouts in their backyards. How far they’re willing to go — including by backing an outright moratorium on development — varies. While many Democratic candidates seem likelier to back a pause, that’s not always the case. And though some Republicans have leaned on party messaging about putting development in local control, rather than supporting a ban, others say a pause is exactly what the moment calls for. Texas gubernatorial and Senate races Deep red Texas has the second-highest number of planned data center projects in the country after Virginia, and across multiple races, data centers have emerged as a key wedge issue. Democratic and Republican candidates are all trying to look tough on data centers but emphasize different messages in their plans. For example, in the Senate race, Democratic candidate and State Rep. James Talarico includes references to environmental impact and sharing corporate profit with the public, while Republican candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton discusses the need to keep Chinese technology out of US data centers. Both, however, want data centers to bear their own energy infrastructure-related costs and want to do away with certain tax exemptions for them. In July, Talarico unveiled his “Hold Data Centers Accountable Plan,” which would end state sales tax incentives, give communities more of a say in data center development, require a closed-loop water system in new data centers to limit consumption, and create federal standards to protect the energy grid and environment. Talarico has also proposed an “AI Dividend” for Americans that would be funded by a tax on “AI-attributable profits.” For his part, Paxton’s “Texas First Data Center Plan,” unveiled in August, would support Gov. Greg Abbott’s state-level policies, including repealing sales tax exemptions for data centers, requiring them to pay for electricity they use and add to state capacity, and preventing AI data centers from building in rural parts of the state. On the federal level, Paxton says he would co-sponsor an existing bill making it easier for data centers to connect to off-grid power systems, introduce new legislation prohibiting the use of Chinese technology to power US data centers or infrastructure, and hold data center companies criminally liable if the facility “empowers AI chatbots that undermine children’s safety.” In the race for the governor’s office, Democratic challenger and State Rep. Gina Hinojosa has accused Abbott, the Republican incumbent, of “flip-flopping” on data centers. Abbott’s office put out a press release last year celebrating a $40 billion Google investment that would include three new data center campuses, but in August 2026, with campaign season heating up, he announced an audit that could slow new facilities connecting to the state energy grid. Hinojosa, who has recently called for a statewide moratorium on data center development, pounced on the perceived inconsistency. “Greg Abbott has zero credibility here. Nobody believes that the arsonist is about to put out the fire,” she said in a social media video. The outcome of these races remains highly uncertain. Cook Political Report changed its rating for the governor’s race earlier this month from a likely Republican win to one that leans Republican. It says the open field for the Senate race is a toss-up. Florida gubernatorial race In Florida, there’s a clash over whether large-scale data centers can be reined in with the right policies or if they should be outright barred in the state. Democratic candidate and former congressman David Jolly has pledged to install a one-year ban on hyperscale data centers on his first day in office, and hasn’t ruled out a permanent extension. In one ad, Jolly puts data centers in the same breath as crime in a list of things he doesn’t want in Florida. His Republican opponent, Congressman Byron Donalds, has previously supported data center development in the state and said Florida is “wide open” to build without destroying the state’s beauty. He’s more recently changed his tune though, and while he still doesn’t want to outright ban data centers, he’s tried to assure voters that he’d support policies protecting them from associated risks like higher energy costs. In July, Donalds introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would require data center developers to fund the energy and water needed to run their operations. He’s also supported a state law with some similar requirements and environmental guardrails. “In my Florida, if you don’t protect our pocketbooks and our people, you won’t build data centers, period,” he assures voters in one ad. Energy experts have warned, however, that Donalds’ pledge to lean on nuclear and natural gas could actually raise costs for consumers. Despite these efforts, he’s been branded as “Data Center Donalds” by opponents, and polling suggests he may have to fight for conservative voters who also strongly oppose data center development. An October NBC6/Telemundo Station Group poll found that 45 percent of likely voter respondents opposed data centers in Florida, with 38 percent in support and 17 percent undecided. A higher percentage opposed data centers in their own communities, at 59 percent. Still, the poll found Donalds has a lead of 48 percent to Jolly’s 41 percent, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percent. Ten percent of respondents were still undecided. Pennsylvania gubernatorial race In one of the country’s relatively few purple states, both candidates for governor have accused each other of changing their rhetoric on data centers just to get votes. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Republican challenger and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity each appear to have hardened their stances amid the widespread backlash to data center development, even though they previously touted opportunity in such projects. Shapiro proudly announced a $20 billion investment from Amazon last year that would bring new data centers to the state, and credited Pennsylvania’s new fast track permitting program in helping lure the investment. But this year, Shapiro has tempered his enthusiasm, signing an executive order in August prohibiting nondisclosure agreements for data center developers and taking AI data center proposals off of the fast track. Shapiro has said his views evolved based on community feedback. But Garrity, too, has seemed to turn against data centers as the election has drawn closer. In a radio interview last year, she said rural parts of the state would be “perfect places to put data centers,” and they’d be largely welcomed based on the economic opportunity they’d bring. She also praised the Amazon investment Shapiro secured at the time, though it’s now a target of some of her attack ads. This year, she has said data center developers must engage the community rather than “jam it down their throats,” and she supports a pause on development lasting no more than three years, according to Spotlight PA. An early October Quinnipiac University poll of likely Pennsylvania voters found 64 percent believed AI data centers in the state would do more harm than good, with a plus or minus 3.9 percent margin of error. But a far larger portion of Democratic respondents were wary of them, with 80 percent saying they’d do more harm than good. That suggests it may be even more essential for Shapiro to shore up his position for his base, though the poll had him leading 59 percent to Garrity’s 34 percent. Ohio Senate race In the battle for Ohio’s Senate seat, data centers are both “the new ingredient (and the new problem),” according to a leaked National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) memo. Republican incumbent Jon Husted and Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown, who’s fighting to win back his former seat, “are in a dead heat,” the NRSC warned in August. And data centers, the group added, “are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.” As the NRSC identified, Brown has made his opposition to data centers a central tenet of his campaign, labeling Husted “the face of data centers” in the state. Brown has hammered Husted over his past support for data centers as lieutenant governor, where he helped install tax breaks. Husted has said he believes local communities should be able to decide whether to bring in data centers, and that some may find the revenue useful. At least as of August, the NRSC still believed voters favored that approach over sweeping bans but acknowledged that current perception is negative. The group warned that losing the Ohio Senate seat could endanger future support for data centers. “If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one,” the memo says. Husted introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would require large load customers like data centers to cover their own energy costs and the infrastructure upgrades needed to accommodate them. The bill passed the House and was seen as a potential life raft for Husted, but narrowly failed to pass the Senate, even with a handful of Democrats voting in favor. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up, and a RealClear Polling average of recent surveys shows Brown with a slight edge. Michigan Senate race Data centers are a hot topic across two key races in Michigan with razor-thin margins. The state is handling dozens of new data center proposals, and both candidates for Michigan’s open Senate seat support a moratorium. Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers supports a one-year pause but opposes a federal ban, while Democratic candidate and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed says there should be “no more data centers until we can do it safely and with federal protections.” Rogers’ moratorium support came days after The Lever reported on his investments that reportedly stand to gain from the buildout. El-Sayed put his stake in the ground on data centers relatively early, compared to other Democrats across the country. In February, Politico wrote that “underdogs” like El-Sayed were centering data centers in their primary campaigns, raising what’s now a common topic in campaign ads. El-Sayed is also now locked in what the Cook Political Report rates as a dead heat with Rogers, in a race that could determine the balance of power in Congress. Rogers and El-Sayed are competing for a seat currently held by Democrat Gary Peters, who isn’t seeking another term. In another toss-up race, Democratic organizer William Lawrence is challenging Republican incumbent Tom Barrett for his House seat. Lawrence called for a year-long federal moratorium on new data center construction during his primary campaign, and when he won the nomination, his supporters reportedly chanted, “data centers lost.” In the general election, data centers have continued to be a central theme. Barrett introduced two bills this summer that would strengthen local decision-making on data center development and bar federal lawmakers from signing non-disclosure agreements about data centers. Lawrence’s data center plan includes environmental standards, worker protections, and “zoning buffers” for data center development. Wisconsin gubernatorial race Wisconsin is another state where both gubernatorial candidates have backed away from previous support for data centers, but neither has gone as far as to call for a moratorium. Democratic nominee and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, for example, set himself apart from his progressive primary opponent Francesca Hong by declining to oppose a development moratorium that she supported. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee, similarly opposes a moratorium in favor of data center guardrails, and voted for a bill allowing faster permitting for data center projects. But Tiffany has still tried to label his opponent as “data center David Crowley,” pointing to past comments he made saying the state shouldn’t “automatically roll back all data center tax incentives.” More recently, Crowley has said he would sign a bill repealing tax subsidies for the facilities. Cook Political Report says the race is a dead heat. Nevada gubernatorial race Nevada’s Democratic Party created an entire website branding Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo “data center Joe,” highlighting his past supportive comments about data centers and money his campaign took from AI-connected donors. Lombardo, locked in a tight race to keep his seat, has fought the accusations. He introduced an executive order last month that ties tax incentives to developers covering power costs and meeting water use standards, empowering the state to claw back money from those who violate it. But Democratic challenger and attorney general Aaron Ford has said he’d go further, pausing tax breaks entirely for new data centers. At the same time, Ford has been criticized for championing a 2015 bill enshrining data center tax breaks. Ford said his thinking has evolved with new information, and that “the data centers of 11 years ago are not the data centers of 2026.” The issue is particularly salient in a state that’s experiencing significant water issues. The Cook Political Report says the race is a toss-up. Georgia gubernatorial race Swing state Georgia has been called “one of the nation’s most attractive markets for AI, hyperscale cloud and enterprise data center development,” and its gubernatorial candidates — Democratic nominee and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican nominee and healthcare executive Rick Jackson — have sparred over each other’s data center records. Bottoms supports a pause on development to evaluate environmental and cost effects, while Jackson says it should be up to local communities to decide whether to bring a data center in. At a recent debate in the toss-up race, Bottoms said her opponent “cannot be trusted” on the topic based on his investment in a Texas data center. Jackson shot back that Bottoms approved and gave tax breaks to multiple data centers as mayor, which Bottoms denied, saying she only approved one non-hyperscale data center that wasn’t near a residential community. While Bottoms led the Invest Atlanta board in 2018, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported, the group approved up to $440 million in bonds for a mixed-use project at Georgia Tech that included a data center. This was not a “direct financing mechanism” but did help the project get tax abatement, the AJC wrote, and its data center was far smaller than those mainly at issue today. Arizona gubernatorial and AG races In dry Arizona where concerns about water are a top issue for many voters, the most interesting conflict is within parties, not across them. Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs and Attorney General Kris Mayes are both locked in close races with their respective Republican challengers, Rep. Andy Biggs and state legislator Warren Petersen. But the two Democrats are split over how to regulate data centers: Mayes supports a statewide pause on development, while Hobbs opposes one. Mayes says the state should “take a beat” to evaluate water and energy needs, a move Petersen has criticized in a rare outright defense of data centers, saying, “If you like your tech and your phone and your computer and the stuff you can use that for, you probably think data centers are important.” Hobbs, meanwhile, says data centers are here to stay, and the state should instead figure out how to best make them work for communities. That puts her significantly closer to her Republican opponent, who similarly opposes a moratorium. Iowa gubernatorial race Iowa’s open governor’s seat is another close race where data centers are taking center stage. The state economic development authority says Iowa’s wind energy and low construction and business costs have attracted developers there, but their growth has also brought concerns to local communities. Democratic nominee and state auditor Rob Sand has not supported a blanket moratorium but says he would end tax breaks for data centers, make them cover their own costs, and keep NDAs from shielding deals from communities. Republican nominee and businessman Zach Lahn called for a moratorium on new development and eliminating tax incentives for them.

articles.title: Brainstacking: Can the latest TikTok trend actually reverse brain rot?
articles.summary: TikTok’s latest trend claims to help combat brain rot and reduce doomscrolling with analog hobbies.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Brainstacking is the latest wellness trend sweeping TikTok , with users sharing a new habit to try to reverse brain rot and stop doomscroolling.

TikTok creator Mandy Rulez popularized the trend, which features users showing off a stack of activities designed to engage the brain and cut down on screen time .

Brainstacking videos showcase aesthetic routines , with creators lighting candles and sipping lattes while showing off a stack of curated activities. There are videos showing people doing this at home, taking a trip to their library and shopping for the perfect aesthetic supplies.

TikTokers show themselves brainstacking in the morning to kick off the day or in the evening to combat job stress and wind down.

The routines vary, but typical activities include journaling, puzzle books like crosswords, Sudoku or Murdle, coloring, and reading nonfiction and fiction books.

Proponents of brainstacking say it boosts brainpower. Critics have called it performative and criticized the use of timed activities rather than more fluid ways of engaging with hobbies.

But can brainstacking really help the brain?

The risks of too much screen time for children are well known. But adults can also feel the negative impacts of spending too much time scrolling, with studies finding that more than two hours of screen time per day can harm learning, memory and mental health, hinder sleep and increase the risk of brain-related diseases like Parkinson’s and dementia .

Social media has been found to be addictive , though even a short break from the apps has been shown to help combat the negative effects.

Do studies back brainstacking activities?

Brain games, like logic puzzles, Sudoku, and crosswords, have long been touted as having cognitive benefits, especially as people age (though most brainstackers are in their 20s). However, the actual research is murkier, with most benefits found in improving specific skill sets rather than overall brain health.

Studies have found an association between cognitively engaging hobbies and a lower risk of cognitive impairment and delayed dementia. But no double-blind, controlled trials exist to prove such a link.

Journaling, a staple in brainstacking, has been shown to have mental and emotional benefits. Studies have shown that writing down our thoughts helps to improve memory, reduce anxiety and depression and ease psychological distress.

Writing by hand, rather than using a digital journal, has proven to improve memory and comprehension and help process emotions.

Coloring has also been shown to benefit adults, supporting mindfulness and stress relief. It may also help with sleep and can improve motor skills.

Reading makes up the centerpiece of many brainstacks. Creators feature both nonfiction and fiction books, focusing on learning and reading for pleasure.

The educational benefits of nonfiction are more self-explanatory: nonfiction books help with critical thinking and offer an opportunity to learn about any subject one desires.

While fiction, especially popular novels , may be viewed as frivolous, studies show that reading fiction improves memory and self-control, strengthens social skills and builds empathy.

articles.title: Marijuana legalization linked to rise in heart-related hospitalizations, study finds
articles.summary: Researchers found heart-related hospitalizations increased after marijuana legalization, raising new questions about cannabis and cardiovascular health.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The legalization of marijuana is linked to a rise in heart-related hospitalizations in the United States, a new study finds.

The research, published in BMJ Open , examined hospitalization rates following ballot measures legalizing cannabis in Western states.

An analysis of more than 50 million hospital discharge records found that hospitalizations for serious heart conditions rose faster after legalization. The research examined hospital discharge diagnosis data from 2012 to 2018.

Admission rates were nearly 4 percent higher for heart failure, 3 percent higher for heart attacks and more than 2 percent higher for atrial fibrillation.

Compared with regions that did not change its laws, the analysis showed that the legalization of cannabis sales across the West beginning in 2014 may have contributed to an increase heart-related hospitalization.

According to the researchers, this is the first study to examine the association between recreational cannabis legalization and cardiovascular hospitalizations.

While researchers found a link between the two, they emphasized that “an observational study cannot prove causality.”

articles.title: Trump says East Potomac renovation will proceed despite judge’s order blocking golf course closure
articles.summary: President Trump is insisting his plan to redevelop East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C., and renovate the public golf course there will be carried out as scheduled despite an order from a federal judge halting future work at the site. In a Truth Social post late Monday, the president said “we are closing the East…
articles.body:
President Trump is insisting his plan to redevelop East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C., and renovate the public golf course there will be carried out as scheduled despite an order from a federal judge halting future work at the site.

In a Truth Social post late Monday, the president said “we are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled” on Nov. 15, saying a judge “does not have the Constitutional Right to ‘ask for or receive notices,’ which are time-consuming, unnecessary, expensive, and unconstitutional.”

The president’s post came hours after U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes granted a preliminary injunction requested by a preservationist group and group of local D.C. golfers asking her to stop the Trump administration from cutting trees at the park as part of the redevelopment project.

“We will immediately appeal this decision,” Trump said. “When completed, it is anticipated that this Course, which will be open to the Public, at a reduced rate for those living in Washington, D.C., will be one of the finest anywhere in the World.”

Trump has enlisted the help of leading golf course architect Tom Fazio on the project, which would transform D.C.’s most widely used public golf course into an 18-hole, championship-length facility he hopes would lure professional tournaments to downtown Washington.

The plan would also eliminate walking and biking trails currently at East Potomac Park, and questions remain about the feasibility of the project and affordability for golfers.

“The Development of this World Championship Public Facility must begin, immediately, if it is to be completed in a timely and seasonal manner,” Trump wrote in his Truth Social post. “To have to give advanced notices to a judge who has no expertise in Golf, Architecture, Landscaping, Construction, or anything else having to do with building such a World Class Project, is not fair, appropriate, or Constitutional.”

For the last several years, East Potomac Golf Links has been operated by the National Links Trust, a local nonprofit that had its lease terminated by the Trump administration last December.

Under the trust, East Potomac Golf Links had become a national model for publicly accessible and affordable golf, particularly catering to junior and beginner golfers.

But Trump and his allies have for months argued changes are needed at the Hains Point property, and the president, who owns dozens of championship courses around the world, can transform the course into a world-renown venue.

“In its current form, the Course is extremely dangerous to play, in that the narrow and nondescript fairways are far too close together, leading to a constant barrage of people being hit with wayward shots, and the echoing throughout the air of the word, ‘FORE,’” Trump wrote in his posts. “The judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project. We are asking the D.C. Circuit Court for immediate remedy.”

articles.title: US government says hackers are now exploiting critical PHP web bugs | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The U.S. government cyber agency warns that hackers have figured out a way to exploit the popular PHP software, used in 70% of the web's software.
articles.body:
U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA has confirmed that hackers are now actively exploiting a pair of critical security vulnerabilities in the widely used PHP web software and has ordered civilian federal agencies within the U.S. government to fix their systems within the next three days.

The urgent new warning to patch comes less than a week after the makers of the decades-old PHP web programming language rolled out patches for the two bugs , which allow hackers to remotely break into a vulnerable system over the internet without the need for passwords. The PHP software is reportedly used by some 70% of web-facing servers, putting major websites and applications at risk. The severity of the bugs prompted some governments and big companies to take their sites offline to fix them.

While the bugs are rated critical, meaning they can be highly damaging if exploited, security researchers said that developing a working exploit to hack into vulnerable systems was initially challenging — but not impossible. Confirmed in-the-wild exploitation now puts extra pressure on organizations to patch their systems to prevent malicious compromises, disruption, and data breaches.

CISA did not provide details about who was exploiting the bugs in its Monday statement , but its statement comes soon after security researchers said they found evidence that the PHP bugs were being exploited .

The bugs, known as PHP2Shell, exploit vulnerabilities in the software that went undiscovered for years. The bugs were initially uncovered two years ago but the nonprofit foundation that maintains the software said there was no practical way for hackers to exploit them, leaving the bugs unpatched. That was until earlier this year, when researchers at security research firm Calif uncovered a way to exploit the two dormant vulnerabilities with the assistance of an AI model.

The two bugs in PHP are among countless vulnerabilities that have not yet been discovered or have been deprioritized for years but now pose a risk due to advances in AI models’ ability to find and exploit vulnerabilities, including by chaining multiple flaws together.

PHP is one of many aging web technologies that help keep the internet and modern technologies running, but that have been under-resourced and under-funded for years , making it difficult for open-source projects like PHP to pay for security reviews that might have uncovered flaws sooner.

articles.title: Trump plans to loosen methane rules for low-producing, high-emitting oil wells
articles.summary: The Trump administration is planning to loosen regulations on methane emissions from the oil and gas sector, and particularly for low-producing, high-emitting oil and gas wells. President Trump will announce a proposed rule to roll back those regulations at a Tuesday night rally in Texas, an administration official confirmed. The draft rule would be expected…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is planning to loosen regulations on methane emissions from the oil and gas sector, and particularly for low-producing, high-emitting oil and gas wells.

President Trump will announce a proposed rule to roll back those regulations at a Tuesday night rally in Texas, an administration official confirmed.

The draft rule would be expected to particularly ease regulations on “marginal wells,” which produce a relatively small quantity of oil or gas.

These oil wells are estimated to produce just 7 percent of the nation’s oil and gas but about half of its methane emissions.

Methane is a planet-warming gas that’s about 28 times more potent than carbon dioxide and is responsible for about 25 percent of global warming.

It mainly comes from the production and transport of fossil fuels — as well as from livestock and other agriculture and decaying waste in landfills. Natural gas is primarily made up of methane.

In addition to cutting back regulations on marginal wells, the administration is also moving to relax rules for the broader oil sector. This includes loosening Biden-era rules that would have phased out some flaring, or the burning off of excess gas during oil production.

The announcement’s timing and details were first reported by Bloomberg . An administration official confirmed the accuracy of the report.

Trump is expected to make the case that the move will encourage more domestic energy production. This has been a priority of the administration, and it comes at a time when high fuel prices pose a challenge for Republicans ahead of the midterm elections.

The president’s appearance is intended to boost Texas Senate candidate and state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) in the major oil-producing state.

The administration expects the changes to save the oil and gas sector $45 billion while allowing an additional 210 million barrels of oil production and 1.41 trillion cubic feet of natural gas from 2027 to 2050. The U.S. consumes about 21 million barrels of oil and 92 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day, so this would mean the equivalent of about 10 days’ worth of oil and 15 days’ worth of gas.

In 2023, the Biden administration tightened methane regulations for oil and gas, a move the administration said would prevent 58 million tons of methane from entering the atmosphere between 2024 and 2038 — the climate equivalent of taking 28 million gas-powered cars off the road for a year.

Previewing the proposed changes earlier this month , the EPA said it also will eliminate the Biden-era Super Emitter Program that would require energy companies to respond to credible reports of major methane leaks.

The administration is still expected to propose repealing that program, which it has already halted.

articles.title: Sanders, Wyden press insurers on Trump ACA coverage terminations
articles.summary: Senate Democrats, led by Sens. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), are pressing 10 major insurance companies about their decisions to work with the Trump administration to terminate coverage for thousands of ObamaCare enrollees due to alleged fraud. The letters, sent Monday to the CEOs of the 10 biggest Affordable Care Act (ACA) insurers…
articles.body:
Senate Democrats, led by Sens. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), are pressing 10 major insurance companies about their decisions to work with the Trump administration to terminate coverage for thousands of ObamaCare enrollees due to alleged fraud.

The letters, sent Monday to the CEOs of the 10 biggest Affordable Care Act (ACA) insurers including Cigna and UnitedHealthcare, question the roles of the companies in the Trump administration’s plan to remove close to 760,000 ACA enrollees as part of its fraud crackdown.

The letters were signed by 11 other Senate Democrats.

“Aligning with Republicans and their so-called ‘war on fraud,’ insurance companies chose to participate in a collaborative effort with the Trump administration to inject yet more chaos and damage into the ACA Marketplace,” the senators wrote.

The pressure on insurance companies for working with the administration is likely a preview of what could happen next year if Democrats flip control of the Senate.

Wyden would become chairman of the Senate Finance Committee while Sanders would chair the Health Committee, both of which have oversight over aspects of the healthcare industry.

“We have many questions about the role of [insurers] in this flawed process used to terminate coverage for 760,000 enrollees, and the judgment exercised by insurance companies that chose to cooperate with CMS officials without requesting clarification about the specific authorities being relied on to support this request or raising concerns to Congress on behalf of their customers,” Wyden and Sanders wrote.

The senators said the administration’s move was based on “discredited, partisan analyses suggesting zero-dollar premium plans and zero-claims enrollees are reliable proxies for fraud.”

According to the senators, the insurance companies sent unsolicited communications, including in some cases asking enrollees to verify their Social Security numbers. Individuals who did not respond were deemed fraudulent and their coverage was terminated.

The senators asked why insurers “almost universally” declined to reach out to enrollees and notify them of significant premium increases ahead of 2026 open enrollment, despite repeated Democratic requests.

“Insurance companies repeatedly cited the complexity and cost associated with initiating new types of mid-year contact with enrollees and delays in finalizing premiums as an explanation for why they were unable to comply with this request,” the senators wrote.

In contrast, enrollee communications were initiated within weeks, if not days, in response to the request from Republicans, they noted.

articles.title: Meta’s $25 billion legal loss just put blood in the water
articles.summary: New Mexico’s $25 billion win in its Cambridge Analytica case against Meta could give states more confidence in bringing tech cases to trial, or seeking larger settlements.
articles.body: When attorneys general from across the US announced a $17 billion settlement with Meta this summer, the sum was unprecedented. But a ruling last week by a New Mexico judge blew that number out of the water. The judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion to resolve claims that Meta misled users around the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal and related incidents. Similar claims were resolved by the settlement with most other states. The outcome raised an obvious question: Should these states have asked for more? The answer depends on a mix of factors, including whether the $25 billion order stands up to Meta’s legal challenges. Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement that the company is “confident we will prevail on appeal” and called New Mexico’s lawsuit an attempt to impose “a tax on speech.” If the fine sticks, however, it could create a new appetite for Big Tech’s opponents to stick it out in court — or ask for bigger payouts to settle. “For the settling AGs, they’re going to look at this and maybe experience some regret for all the claims that they waived, and start looking around and trying to figure out what’s left that they didn’t waive, if they can try to get some money like this too,” says Daphne Keller, director of platform regulation at the Stanford Program in Law, Science & Technology. For the many individuals, school districts, and tribes with outstanding claims, “this is very encouraging and will make them hopeful that continuing to litigate aggressively will lead to a big payout,” Keller says. The $25 billion court order covered millions of violations of New Mexico’s unfair practices law, after a jury found Meta had misled users about how it protected their data and policed misinformation and hate speech – claims stemming from the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal. In most states, such claims were covered by a section of the kids online safety settlement, resolved with a $459 million payment. While that number looks comparatively puny, there were upsides to taking it. A settlement provided more certainty and an expedited payout for states even though Meta will be making the payments over 10 years. It also secured product commitments from Meta, like restrictions on teen usage, that might have been more difficult to get from a court ruling. And it allowed those to be implemented soon after the settlement was approved, which advocates say is important to prevent further harm to kids. Other state attorneys general also may have been working with different laws or evidence that could result in outcomes different from those obtained in New Mexico. But New Mexico’s win, combined with other recent legal victories for AGs and private plaintiffs — including a separate judgment of nearly $1 billion against Meta in New Mexico — may embolden anyone still litigating privacy and kids online safety cases. “Assuming that even a fraction of this award gets upheld, then they clearly took pennies on the dollar compared to New Mexico,” Keller says of the settling states. Imagining she’s an AG with similar claims — like public false statements about privacy or content moderation — “I become less willing to settle in those cases,” Keller adds. “Or if I do settle, I ask for more.” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, whose state avoided joining the Meta settlement, seemed to take the latest New Mexico ruling as a validation. “As I said at the time, the multi-state settlement with Meta was a slap on the wrist,” Utheimer wrote on X. “Florida isn’t going to sell out to Meta. We’re going to hold them accountable.” The District of Columbia could be the next place to test whether New Mexico’s win can be replicated since it did not settle its Cambridge Analytica claims and has continued pursuing its lawsuit in court. While the AGs who joined the settlement can’t pursue covered claims against Meta anymore, they could still push for more in cases against other social media defendants, including TikTok, YouTube, and Snap. And those who weren’t part of the Meta settlement, including school districts and individuals, may be encouraged to continue pushing ahead. “Realistically, there’s so many cases, it’s not feasible that every single case can have an outcome like this,” says Keller. “Meta actually would go broke because the multipliers are so large. But any one, or 10, or 50 of them could hit the jackpot.” States have stepped in to pursue tech policy and competition cases where the federal government has declined to, but the wide range of potential outcomes for each state presents its own challenges. As Congress has stalled on major tech policy bills and the Trump administration has often favored lighter regulation on tech, Colorado Law associate professor Blake Reid sees recent cases as a “move toward state-level tech policy.” “The trick of that is, now you have 50 states that all have different sets of resources, and different sets of politics, and different sets of incentives, and frankly just different skill levels in terms of the sophistication that it takes to do litigation at this scale,” Reid says. “And it’s the same Meta, but now it’s up to 50 small opponents that are going to break in different ways.” As for whether the $25 billion ruling makes other states rethink their strategy, Reid says there could be a range of approaches, depending partly on whether the figure is upheld on appeal and whether Meta loses yet more cases. “Is that a game that every state attorney general wants to play?” he asks. “And I think the settlement in the other case suggests maybe not.” Still, the new figure may change what AGs think they can achieve in court. And the more losses Meta and other tech companies rack up, the more ambitious they might get.

articles.title: UK charges 2 British men over security incident at US-operated air base
articles.summary: The United Kingdom on Tuesday announced it has charged two British men in connection to a suspected plot to attack a U.S.-run air base last month, an incident the country has blamed on Iran. The British police charged Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim, 24, from London, under the National Security Act with conduct to assist a foreign…
articles.body:
The United Kingdom on Tuesday announced it has charged two British men in connection to a suspected plot to attack a U.S.-run air base last month, an incident the country has blamed on Iran.

The British police charged Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim, 24, from London, under the National Security Act with conduct to assist a foreign intelligence service, according to a release from the Crown Prosecution Service .

“In this case, we believe that country to be Iran,” Laurence Taylor, the head of British counterterrorism policing, later said in a statement.

Authorities charged a second British man, Nouman Essghir, 24, also under the National Security Act with entering, accessing, inspecting or approaching a “prohibited place” for reasons “prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom” on Aug. 22.

The two men on Tuesday morning appeared in a London courtroom.

Essghir was one of five men initially arrested outside the RAF Fairford air base in the early hours of Sept. 27. The military installation is owned by the U.K. but operated by the U.S., which has positioned its B-1 bombers there to carry out strikes on Iran. Washington withdrew the bombers because of security concerns shortly after the incident in Gloucestershire, England.

Notably, however, Essghir was charged in connection with activity that U.K. authorities accused him of carrying out more than a month before the RAF incident.

Iran has denied its involvement in the incident outside the air base.

“We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state,” Taylor said.

“As the director general of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat,” he added, referring to the U.K.’s domestic security agency.

Five other men arrested in the case remain released on bail, a move for which President Trump has criticized the U.K.

Taylor admitted the men’s release “sparked significant questions and speculation about the investigation and why that was the case,” but he said it led to “swifter progress, better evidence and ultimately us securing the charges.”

“We know that decisions made during our investigations can sometimes appear illogical to those on the outside, but I want to make it very clear that there will always be good reason or rationale behind them,” he said.

articles.title: Trump is making it easier for fossil fuel companies to leak methane
articles.summary: The Trump administration wants to undo guardrails against methane leaks at oil and gas wells as data centers demand more energy.
articles.body: In its latest gift to oil and gas companies, the Trump administration is expected to announce plans today to weaken rules that guard against methane leaks. Methane is a smog-forming pollutant and a powerful greenhouse gas that’s up to 80 times as potent as carbon dioxide on a 20-year horizon. It’s the primary component of what the fossil fuel industry calls “natural gas” that routinely leaks from oil and gas wells and pipelines. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is reversing course on its previous efforts to plug those leaks. As part of President Donald Trump’s deregulatory agenda, the EPA plans to undo Biden-era rules that were expected to cut methane emissions by 80 percent over 14 years. The EPA teased the rule change earlier this month, saying in a press release that it was “days away” from making the proposal. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin says the rollbacks will save oil and gas companies $45 billion, while the previous rules would have incurred $18 billion in regulatory costs. “This proposal takes on many of the problems American [oil and gas] producers and operators have raised with us,” Zeldin said in the October 7th press release. “The Trump EPA is committed to fixing this so the U.S. can reach its full energy potential.” The agency is expected to step back standards for so-called “marginal wells” — old wells that produce little fuel but create an outsize amount of methane pollution from leaks. These wells are responsible for half of the industry’s methane emissions despite only producing 6 percent of US oil and gas, ProPublica reports. The EPA is also expected to end the Super Emitter Program that notified oil and gas infrastructure operators of large releases of methane reaching 100 kilograms per hour or more. Trump plans to make the announcement from a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, today, Bloomberg reports. Not only is Texas the top oil- and gas-producing state in the US, it’s also the world’s biggest data center market. With more data center capacity under construction than any other state, Texas has become emblematic of the challenges energy-intensive AI models pose. In just five years, data centers could undo decades of air quality improvements in Texas, according to a recent report by the Houston Advanced Research Center. Methane has caused about 30 percent of global warming so far. But unlike carbon dioxide, which can linger in the atmosphere for hundreds or thousands of years, methane dissipates in a little over a decade. That makes eliminating methane emissions, particularly from unintentional leaks, one of the fastest and most straightforward ways to stop global temperatures from rising. The EPA’s rollbacks quickly triggered furor from health and environmental advocates. “Any proposed rollback to the federal methane rule is a slap in the face to families who are exposed to oil and gas pollution where they live, work, and play,” Celerah Hewes, a senior manager for state field campaigns at Moms Clean Air Force, said in an email ahead of the expected announcement. “For over a decade, [our group] has been fighting for methane protections for our families—and we were making progress. Today’s announcement from EPA is a massive blow to the efforts to safeguard our children’s health and our climate.” The Biden-era methane rules were estimated to bring in up to $98 billion in benefits by reducing climate risks and health costs from air pollution, even after factoring in the costs of compliance. Plugging leaks was supposed to lead to up to $13 billion worth of recovered natural gas.

Shuford, an infectious disease physician, was a former Texas health commissioner. She was appointed in April as part of a leadership team to support director Erica Schwartz,…
articles.body:
Dr. Jennifer Shuford, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) deputy director and chief medical officer, is leaving the agency after just four months on the job.

Shuford, an infectious disease physician, was a former Texas health commissioner. She was appointed in April as part of a leadership team to support director Erica Schwartz, along with Sean Slovenski as CDC’s chief operating officer.

Shuford will stay on until just after the midterm elections. Her last day at CDC will be Nov. 12, the agency said.

“I am leaving to spend more time with my family. I am so thankful to President Trump and Secretary Kennedy for giving me the opportunity to help lead CDC. It has been an amazing experience and I will be forever grateful for it,” Shuford said in a statement.

Satish Pillai, a career public health official, will serve as the agency’s acting deputy director and chief medical officer while the CDC looks for a permanent replacement. CDC said it will “initiate the process of identifying a permanent successor in the near future.”

Shuford’s departure comes as CDC faces criticism over the nation’s continuously spreading measles outbreak, as well as a dispute with Pennsylvania over the agency’s refusal to acknowledge several measles-related deaths.

As chief medical officer, Shuford would have been directly involved in determining how the agency defines a measles death. She also coordinated the CDC’s response to the Ebola outbreak in Africa and was involved in the decision to quarantine overseas Americans exposed to the virus instead of repatriating them.

“I imagine that she has found her red line,” Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who resigned from the agency in protest in August 2025, told The Hill in a text message. “She is an excellent public health leader. I fear what is to come next.”

During her time in Texas, Shuford gained respect from career CDC career staff as she coordinated the state’s response to a measles outbreak last year.

“I am deeply grateful for Dr. Shuford’s outstanding leadership and commitment to CDC and public health, especially as she has navigated an exceptionally demanding, high-profile, and constantly evolving environment over the past several months,” Schwartz said in a statement.

articles.body:
Prediction market platform Kalshi is expanding protections for young traders aged 18-20, which includes a new monthly deposit limit.

Accounts in the age range will now have a $2,500 monthly deposit limit, Kalshi announced in a press release Tuesday. They will be automatically placed into “special accounts” that will have extra protections and built-in responsible trading education.

“Like the stock exchange, Kalshi is available only to traders 18 and older,” said Luana Lopes Lara, COO and co-founder of Kalshi in the release. “Still, we know that young adults are often new to markets and may need more education and safeguards, so we are expanding our protections for this group of users.”

The company also announced new partnerships with organizations — Parent ProTech and ConnectSafely — to publish a Parents’ Guides to Prediction Markets, according to the release.

“The guides will give parents everything they need to know to ensure responsible trading habits and keep minors off of Kalshi,” the release said.

Among the new features announced is also a trade alert, which will pop up when a new trader with a balance over $1,000 puts more than 25 percent of that balance in a single trade, encouraging them to diversify their trading.

Digital safety for kids amid the growing popularity of prediction markets has been a rising concern in Congress , with several lawmakers introducing legislation to protect minors.

Earlier this year, a bipartisan pair of senators introduced legislation to ban digital gambling advertisements that target minors. The bill, sponsored by Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Katie Britt (R-Ala.), aimed to establish a federal ban on sports betting ads on social media platforms like Instagram or TikTok.

Before that, Blumenthal introduced another bill in March that was aimed at preventing abuse and fraud in prediction markets.

In May, Kalshi introduced a new initiative making face ID the default for users who already have it enabled on their phones. The platform also encouraged parents to use Kalshi with two-factor authentication to prevent their kids from accessing their accounts.

articles.title: DCCC pushes for ads targeting GOP on AI, data centers in dozens of key House races
articles.summary: The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) is pushing for advertising targeting Republican candidates over their record on AI and data centers in dozens of key House races, as technology-related issues take on new significance in the midterm elections. In a report shared first with The Hill, the Tech Oversight Project noted that House Democrats’ official…
articles.body:
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) is pushing for advertising targeting Republican candidates over their record on AI and data centers in dozens of key House races, as technology-related issues take on new significance in the midterm elections.

In a report shared first with The Hill, the Tech Oversight Project noted that House Democrats’ official campaign arm is seeking to put an emphasis on AI and data centers in almost half of the races it is targeting.

Thirty-one out of the DCCC’s 69 “redboxes,” which lay out potential messaging in key races, mention GOP candidates’ prior support for data center tax incentives, as well as investments in and contributions from developers of the controversial AI infrastructure.

“For the first time, the balance of power in Congress will be determined by how voters feel about Big Tech and AI,” Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, said in a statement.

Tech-related issues have not often risen to the forefront of electoral politics. But as Americans are becoming increasingly wary of the push to rapidly build new data centers in support of AI, they have become a bigger target in the upcoming midterms.

The DCCC is highlighting data center talking points in races against Republican incumbents like Reps. Eli Crane (Ariz.), Bill Huizenga (Mich.), Bryan Steil (Wis.) and Mike Lawler (N.Y.).

In Huizenga’s case, they suggest “voters should see aggressive, hard-hitting ads” in the Grand Rapids, Mich., media market about his support for “unleashing data centers across Michigan.”

For Steil, the House Democrats’ campaign arm says “voters district wide, but especially in the Madison media market, need to read mail about how” the congressman has received support from PACs tied to data center developers.

Some Democratic candidates appear to have received the message. Montana House candidate Sam Forstag took aim at his Republican opponent Aaron Flint in an ad targeting his record on both AI and data centers.

“If Democrats take back control of Congress, they need to govern how they campaigned: by putting Big Tech to the sword, investigating them for corruption, and rolling back the handouts and giveaways that Republicans gave them,” Haworth added.

articles.body:
The Federal Election Commission’s electronic filing system has been down for hours on Tuesday, according to a spokesperson who confirmed the agency’s IT teams are working to restore the service.

According to the FEC’s incident update page, the agency said Monday night it is “investigating this issue,” stating the FEC filing system is down. An update shortly after 9:30 a.m. EDT Tuesday said the agency is “continuing to investigate this issue.”

“At this time, we can point to the status update posted to the FEC’s website that the electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service,” the spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill.

The FEC’s website search function used to find campaign donations, recipients and political action committee information is not impacted by the outage.

It is not clear what caused the outage, though Reuters , citing an email, reported the FEC website was targeted by a hacker or hackers.

The incident comes just over a week until voters across the country will head to the polls for the midterm elections. The FEC’s functions should not impact the electoral process.

articles.title: CFTC sues to block Utah from enforcing gambling laws against prediction markets
articles.summary: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) announced on Tuesday that it has filed a lawsuit against the state of Utah to stop the state’s efforts to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets. The lawsuit follows a lengthy battle the state has been fighting against prediction markets. In August, a federal judge in Utah ruled that the…
articles.body:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) announced on Tuesday that it has filed a lawsuit against the state of Utah to stop the state’s efforts to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets.

The lawsuit follows a lengthy battle the state has been fighting against prediction markets. In August , a federal judge in Utah ruled that the Commodities Exchange Act does not block Utah from enforcing its gambling restrictions against prediction markets.

Enacted in the 1930s, the Commodities Exchange Act was updated after the 2008 financial crisis to give the CFTC the ability to regulate financial instruments known as swaps.

“Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets,” said CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig in a press release on Tuesday. “Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes—they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets.”

In February, CFTC-regulated prediction market platform Kalshi sued Utah Gov. Spencer Cox (R) and other state officials seeking to block a potential enforcement action. Utah is one of the few states in the country that bans all forms of gambling.

Selig announced earlier this year the CFTC would challenge any state’s attempt to regulate prediction markets, sparking a response from Cox, who said he would “use every resource within my disposal as governor of the sovereign state of Utah, and under the Constitution of the United States to beat you in court.”

Utah sued Kalshi this month alleging that the platform “lets Utahns bet on sports, elections, politics and other outcomes, and that this violates Utah’s gambling laws,” according to a press release from the office of Utah Attorney General Derek Brown.

“Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Brown said in the release.

In Tuesday’s announcement, the CFTC said, “if a state challenges the lawful operation of a derivatives exchange, the Commission will protect federal sovereign interests.”

“This action reflects the CFTC’s firm commitment to maintaining its exclusive jurisdiction over CFTC-registered prediction markets,” the release continued.
